conventional_description: Vitiligo is a chronic skin condition where patches of skin lose their pigment. It happens when melanocytes, the cells that produce melanin, are destroyed or stop functioning. The exact cause isn't fully understood, but it's considered an autoimmune disorder, often associated with other autoimmune conditions like thyroid disease. Diagnosis is usually made by visual examination, sometimes with a Wood's lamp to highlight depigmented areas.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment focuses on restoring color to the skin or evening out skin tone. Options include topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors to reduce inflammation, narrowband UVB phototherapy to stimulate melanocytes, and in some cases, oral immunosuppressants. For extensive vitiligo, depigmentation of remaining pigmented skin may be considered. Cosmetic camouflage is also a common approach.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the skin is not an isolated organ - it's a mirror of the body's internal balance, particularly the state of Qi, Blood, and the organ systems that produce them. The Liver stores Blood and ensures its smooth flow; the Kidneys store Essence, which fuels the production of Blood; the Spleen transforms food into Qi and Blood. When any of these systems are out of balance, the skin may lose its nourishment and pigment. This is why vitiligo is never just a skin problem in TCM - it's a signal that something deeper is stuck, depleted, or invaded.
Emotional stress, for example, can cause Liver Qi Stagnation, where the energy that should be moving Blood to the skin gets blocked. Over time, this stagnation can lead to Blood Stagnation, where the actual blood flow in the tiny vessels under the skin is impaired.
In other cases, a constitutional weakness in the Kidneys or Spleen means the body simply can't produce enough Blood to reach the skin's surface. And sometimes, a deficiency of Blood leaves the skin vulnerable to an invasion of external Wind, which further disrupts local circulation. Each of these patterns produces a slightly different type of white patch - some well-defined, some blurry, some itchy - and each requires a different treatment strategy.
That's why a TCM diagnosis doesn't stop at 'vitiligo.' The practitioner will ask about your energy, digestion, emotions, and sleep, and examine your tongue and pulse to identify which pattern is at play. The goal is to restore the internal harmony that allows the skin to heal itself.
classical_quote: 「白癜者，面及颈项身体皮肉色变白，与肉色不同，亦不痒痛，谓之白癜。」
classical_translation: "Vitiligo is a condition where the skin of the face, neck, and body turns white, differing from the normal flesh color, without itching or pain; this is called white patches."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Causes and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Chapter on Bai Dian (White Patches) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by observing the white patches closely - their color, border clarity, and whether they itch or burn - and then asks about your overall health, emotions, and energy. The tongue and pulse offer a deeper layer of confirmation, because each pattern leaves a distinct imprint on these diagnostic signs.
When the patches are well-defined, may itch or burn, and the complexion looks darkish, the pattern is Qi and Blood Stagnation. The tongue is purple with stasis spots and the pulse feels wiry and choppy, indicating that both Qi and Blood are stuck, often with internal Wind causing the itching. This pattern arises when emotional stress or trauma blocks the flow, depriving the skin of nourishment.
When patches clearly worsen with emotional stress - accompanied by chest distension, sighing, or menstrual irregularities - that signals Liver Qi Stagnation. The tongue body stays pale-red with a thin white coat, but the pulse becomes distinctly wiry, reflecting the constrained energy that fails to move Blood smoothly to the skin.
Long-standing stagnation can deepen into Blood Stagnation. Here the white patches are sharply defined, the complexion may look dark, and the tongue turns purplish with stasis spots. The pulse feels wiry or choppy, as if it stumbles over obstacles. This tells the practitioner that blood flow in the tiny skin vessels is physically blocked.
When fatigue, poor appetite, and loose stools accompany dull, poorly defined white patches, the root is often Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency. The tongue appears pale with little coating, and the pulse is thin and weak. Without enough Qi to generate blood and nourish the skin, the patches remain faint and ill-defined.
A chronic, deep deficiency pattern is Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency. The patches are porcelain-white or irregular, and the person may feel dizzy, have tinnitus, a sore back, and dry eyes. The tongue is red with little coating, and the pulse is thin or deep and rapid. This reflects a fundamental lack of essence to moisten and color the skin.
If the patches are dry and itchy with a thin tongue coating and a wiry pulse, consider Blood Deficiency with External Wind. The skin lacks proper Blood nourishment, making it vulnerable to Wind lodging in the surface, which triggers the itching and the pale, dry appearance of the spots.

patterns.symptoms: ["Milky or porcelain-white patches, often with whitened hairs", "Dizziness and ringing in the ears", "Soreness and weakness of the lower back and knees", "Night sweats and heat in the palms, soles, and chest", "Insomnia with vivid dreams", "Dry eyes and blurred vision"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, Overwork and lack of sleep, Spicy, greasy foods, Excessive sweating (sauna, hot yoga), Alcohol
patterns.better_with: Adequate sleep and rest, Cool, hydrating foods (pear, cucumber), Goji berries and black sesame, Gentle exercise, Stress reduction
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver stores Blood and the Kidney stores Essence; together they nourish the skin and hair. When Liver and Kidney Yin become deficient, Essence and Blood are depleted, failing to provide the nourishment needed to maintain normal pigment. This leads to the gradual appearance of milky-white patches, often with whitening of hair, while systemic signs like dizziness, tinnitus, and lower-back soreness confirm the root deficiency.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine, rapid, and wiry; left Chi (Kidney) position weak, left Guan (Liver) thin.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Liver and Kidney Yin deficiency means the body's cooling, moistening reserves are low. Stress, overwork, and late nights further consume Yin, while spicy and heating foods generate internal heat that dries up fluids. Rest, cooling foods, and stress reduction help conserve and rebuild Yin, allowing Essence to once again nourish the skin and restore pigment.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and a regular sleep schedule to preserve Yin. Eat Yin-nourishing foods like black sesame seeds, goji berries, walnuts, and black beans. Avoid spicy, fried, and overly heating foods, and limit alcohol and caffeine. Gentle exercise such as walking or Tai Chi is beneficial, but avoid excessive sweating that depletes fluids.

patterns.symptoms: ["White patches worsen with emotional stress", "Chest or rib-side distension", "Frequent sighing", "Irritability or mood swings", "Irregular or painful menstruation", "Tongue sides red or slightly purple"]
patterns.worse_with: Anger or frustration, Emotional stress, Alcohol, Spicy, greasy foods, Sedentary lifestyle
patterns.better_with: Stress reduction, Gentle exercise, Warm, light meals, Open communication
patterns.why_this_happens: Your Liver is responsible for keeping Qi flowing smoothly throughout your body. When emotional stress, frustration, or anger build up, that flow gets stuck - a state called Liver Qi Stagnation. The stagnant Qi can no longer properly push Blood and nourishment up to the skin, leaving patches of skin undernourished and unable to produce pigment. This is why the white patches often appear or worsen during times of emotional upset, and why they may improve when you feel calm and balanced.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly dark body, red or slightly purple sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), like a taut guitar string.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress and anger are the classic triggers that knot up Liver Qi, directly driving the stagnation that starves the skin of nourishment. Alcohol and greasy, spicy foods add heat and dampness, further clogging the Liver's smooth flow. Calming practices, gentle movement, and a clean diet untie that knot, allowing Qi and Blood to reach the skin again.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Make stress reduction a daily practice - gentle yoga, walking, or meditation can help keep Liver Qi moving. Limit alcohol, coffee, and spicy or greasy foods, which can add heat to an already stagnant Liver. Eat plenty of leafy greens, and try adding a little mint or rose tea to your routine to gently lift the Qi.

patterns.symptoms: ["White patches with clear, sometimes hyperpigmented borders", "Dusky or dark facial complexion", "Dark purplish lips and nails", "Fixed, stabbing pain that worsens at night", "Dark menstrual blood with clots (in women)", "Rough, dry, scaly skin"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold weather or exposure, Sedentary lifestyle, Emotional suppression, Injury or trauma to skin
patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise, Warmth, Stress reduction, Warm, spiced foods
patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi flow is blocked for a long time-often from stress, injury, or chronic illness-blood cannot circulate smoothly. This stagnation in the skin's tiny vessels (collaterals) starves the melanocytes of nourishment, leading to well-defined white patches. The stasis also causes the skin around the patches to darken and may produce a dusky complexion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended dark sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 Sè) or wiry (弦 Xián).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold congeals blood, while warmth and movement encourage circulation. Stagnation often starts with constrained Liver Qi, so emotional release and gentle exercise prevent the buildup that leads to blood stasis. Injury can physically block the vessels, triggering local patches.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, moving foods like turmeric, black pepper, cinnamon, and small amounts of red meat. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks that congeal blood. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi keeps Qi and blood flowing; avoid prolonged sitting. Manage stress with meditation or journaling, as emotional tension worsens stagnation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When emotional stress or other factors cause Qi to become stuck, it can no longer propel Blood smoothly through the body. Over time, this stagnation creates a blockage in the tiny vessels (collaterals) that feed the skin, depriving melanocytes of the nourishment they need to produce pigment. The result is well‑defined white patches, often accompanied by itching as stagnant Qi and Blood generate internal Wind.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dark body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress directly stagnates Liver Qi, which is the engine of Blood movement-so frustration, anger, or resentment make the stasis worse. Cold constricts vessels and slows circulation, while gentle exercise and warmth dilate them and encourage flow. Greasy, spicy foods can generate internal Heat and Dampness that further gum up the collaterals. By contrast, a calm mind and regular movement keep Qi unblocked, allowing Blood to reach the skin and restore its color.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle, daily movement like walking or tai chi helps keep Qi and Blood flowing. Avoid prolonged sitting and tight clothing that can restrict circulation. Manage stress with meditation or deep breathing-emotional tension directly worsens this pattern. Eat warm, lightly cooked foods and limit cold, raw, or greasy items that can congeal Blood.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, milky-white patches with blurry edges", "Fatigue and physical weakness that worsens with exertion", "Poor appetite or dislike of eating", "Abdominal bloating after meals", "Loose or unformed stools", "Sallow or pale complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Skipping meals or irregular eating, Raw, cold, and iced foods, Overwork and lack of sleep, Excessive worry or pensiveness, Greasy, heavy meals
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Adequate sleep and rest, Gentle exercise, Small, frequent meals
patterns.why_this_happens: Your Spleen and Stomach are like a kitchen that turns food into Qi and Blood, the vital substances that nourish every inch of your skin. When they are weak, this production line slows down, and the skin is starved of the nourishment it needs to maintain its color. The white patches that result are dull and poorly defined because the deficiency is widespread, not trapped in one spot. The fatigue, poor appetite, and loose stools you may feel are the very same digestive weakness showing up in other ways.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with tooth marks on the edges and a thin white coating. Pulse: overall weak and soft, especially the right middle (guan) position, which feels empty and lacks force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on routine and warmth. Skipping meals or eating cold, raw foods forces it to work harder to warm and break down what you eat, further depleting its Qi. Overwork and worry also directly injure Spleen Qi in TCM, which is why stress can worsen digestive symptoms and, by extension, the white patches. Warm, cooked foods and regular rest take the burden off the Spleen, allowing it to rebuild the Qi and Blood that eventually reach and recolor the skin.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congee, soups, and stewed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the digestive fire. Eat at regular times, chew thoroughly, and stop before you feel full. Gentle movement like walking or taichi after meals supports Qi flow without draining energy.

patterns.worse_with: Exposure to wind and drafts, Cold weather or exposure, Emotional stress, Overwork and lack of sleep, Poor diet (raw, cold, or spicy foods)
patterns.better_with: Warmth, Adequate sleep and rest, Nourishing, warm foods, Gentle exercise, Moisturizing the skin
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's Blood is deficient, the skin loses its nourishment, becoming dry, pale, and fragile. This weakness allows external Wind to invade and lodge in the skin, disrupting the local flow of Qi and Blood. The combination of malnourished skin and pathogenic Wind leads to the appearance of dry, itchy white patches (vitiligo) that may shift or change over time.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white and slightly dry coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and wiry, possibly floating at the front position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Deficiency leaves the skin undernourished and vulnerable, so external Wind easily invades and causes itching and depigmentation. Warmth and rest conserve Blood and Qi, while nourishing foods directly replenish Blood. Gentle movement encourages circulation without depleting resources. Conversely, wind exposure aggravates the external pathogen, cold constricts and slows blood flow, stress and overwork consume Blood, and poor diet fails to build the necessary Blood to protect and moisten the skin.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat nourishing blood-building foods like dark leafy greens, beets, black sesame, bone broth, eggs, and moderate amounts of organ meats. Avoid raw, cold, and spicy foods that can disrupt digestion and stir up Wind. Protect the skin from cold and wind with appropriate clothing, and keep the skin moisturized. Gentle exercise like Tai Chi or walking helps move Qi and Blood without overexertion. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork to preserve Blood.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure vitiligo?
faqs.answer: TCM does not promise a cure, but it aims to address the root imbalance that allows the white patches to appear. Many patients experience repigmentation, especially on the face and trunk, and a halt in spreading. The goal is long-term stability and restored skin color by harmonizing the body's internal systems.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results?
faqs.answer: Most people notice a subtle change - such as a slight darkening at the edges of a patch or a stop in spreading - within 3 to 4 months of consistent treatment. Full repigmentation is a longer process, often taking 6 to 18 months, and some stubborn areas like hands and feet may respond more slowly.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside phototherapy?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is often used alongside narrowband UVB or other light therapies. In fact, some herbs may enhance the skin's response to light. Always inform both your dermatologist and your TCM practitioner about all treatments you're receiving to coordinate care safely.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet is an important part of TCM treatment. You'll likely be advised to avoid greasy, fried, and sugary foods that create dampness and heat, and to eat more warm, cooked meals. Foods that nourish Blood and Essence, like black sesame seeds, goji berries, and dark leafy greens, are often recommended to support skin health.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with vitiligo?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be adapted for children. Herbal doses are adjusted for age and weight, and acupuncture may use gentler techniques or be replaced with acupressure. Always work with a practitioner experienced in pediatric care, and keep your child's pediatrician informed.

faqs.question: What if my patches are spreading quickly?
faqs.answer: Rapid spreading indicates an active internal imbalance, often related to a strong emotional trigger or a pathogenic factor like Wind. TCM can help calm this acute phase by addressing the underlying pattern - for example, by soothing the Liver or expelling Wind - while also working on the long-term root. However, if the spread is accompanied by other alarming symptoms, please see the Safety section for when to seek urgent medical care.

research.title: Expert consensus on TCM diagnosis and treatment of vitiligo
research.description: A national expert consensus document outlining the main TCM patterns for vitiligo (Qi and Blood Disharmony, Liver Qi Stagnation, Spleen and Stomach Deficiency, Channel and Collateral Stasis, and Liver and Kidney Deficiency), along with recommended herbal formulas, acupuncture points, and external therapies. It serves as the primary clinical reference for TCM practitioners in China.
research.periodical: China Association of Chinese Medicine, Dermatology Branch. Expert consensus on TCM diagnosis and treatment of vitiligo. Chinese Journal of Dermatology, 2020.

research.title: Analysis of TCM formulas and patterns for vitiligo
research.description: This study reviewed a large collection of TCM prescriptions for vitiligo and found that the most common patterns were Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency (16%), Blood Stasis and Channel Obstruction (10%), Liver Qi Stagnation (8%), and Qi and Blood Disharmony (6%). The most frequently used single herbs included He Shou Wu, Nu Zhen Zi, Dang Gui, and Chuan Xiong.
research.periodical: Wang X, et al. Analysis of TCM formulas and patterns for vitiligo. Frontiers in Chinese Medicine Research, 2022.

research.title: Acupuncture treatment of vitiligo: clinical observation
research.description: A clinical report from the China Association of Acupuncture-Moxibustion describing a protocol combining body acupuncture (Fengchi GB-20, Quchi LI-11, Hegu LI-4, Sanyinjiao SP-6, Taichong LR-3), local plum-blossom needling of white patches, and ear acupressure. The total effective rate was reported as over 90%, with best results in early, localized cases.
research.periodical: China Association of Acupuncture-Moxibustion. Acupuncture treatment of vitiligo: clinical observation. CAAM website, 2021.
